For You

Start with your situation, not medical terminology.

You do not have to understand everything at once. Choose the information you need most—without assumptions about your status, relationships or how you should feel.

Choose a path

What are you looking for?

  • I recently learned I am living with HIV→
  • I am considering an HIV test→

There is no single “right” path.

Read one section, move between sections or return later. This page does not ask for personal information.

I recently learned I am living with HIV

You remain your whole self.

HIV status is health information. It does not determine your worth, character, ability, relationships or future.

Next steps may include connecting with care, understanding antiretroviral therapy (ART), and discussing a testing and care plan with a health professional. ART suppresses HIV in the body. Viral load describes the amount of HIV in the blood, while a CD4 test helps assess one part of immune health.

When ART is effective and an undetectable viral load is maintained, HIV is not sexually transmitted—a principle known as U=U.

Questions you can take to a health service

  • When can I start or continue ART?
  • Which tests are needed and how will the results be explained?
  • When will my viral load be checked?
  • Who can help if I have side effects or find it difficult to take treatment?
  • How is my health information kept confidential?
Understand ART, viral load & CD4Understand U=U
You do not need to decide everything today.

Start with what you need most. For clinical decisions, ask a qualified health professional who understands your circumstances.

I am considering an HIV test

Testing helps you know your status; it does not judge you.

An HIV test is the way to determine HIV status. The test type and time since a possible exposure affect when a result can be relied upon.

One reactive result is not a final diagnosis; confirmatory testing is required under the national algorithm by trained personnel. When a test is taken close to a possible exposure, a provider can explain the window period—the time when some tests may not yet detect infection.

  • Ask which test is being used and what the result means.
  • Ask whether and when retesting is needed.
  • Ask how confidentiality is protected.
  • Request an explanation of next steps for any result.

My partner is living with HIV

Information and respect help partners make decisions together.

HIV status does not remove anyone’s right to privacy, autonomy, relationships or a future.

  • Understand U=U

    A maintained undetectable viral load through effective treatment means HIV is not sexually transmitted.

  • Communicate without blame

    Ask what your partner wants to discuss. Do not turn every conversation into a check on medication or health status.

  • Make shared decisions

    Testing, prevention, contraception or pregnancy planning can be discussed with a qualified provider based on each person’s circumstances and choices.

  • Respect privacy and autonomy

    Do not share a partner’s status without consent. Support does not mean taking over their health decisions.

My friend or family member is living with HIV

Listening is often more useful than immediately offering advice.

“Thank you for trusting me. What kind of support would help?”

Protect confidentiality. Avoid blaming questions. Do not demand medical details. When you hear a myth, correct the information without turning the person into a teaching example.

I want to be more supportive

Support can be visible in small choices of words and action.

  • Listen before responding.

    Let the person decide what to share and what support they want.

  • Use accurate information.

    Know how HIV can and cannot be transmitted, and understand U=U.

  • Protect confidentiality.

    Someone’s HIV status is not our story to tell.

  • Respect choices.

    Do not pressure someone to educate others, disclose their status or accept a particular kind of help.

  • See the whole person.

    Do not make a diagnosis the centre of every conversation.

Simple phrases that may help

“I am here to listen.”

“What do you need from me right now?”

“This information stays with me.”

HIV

I simply want to learn

Responsible curiosity can help reduce stigma.

Start with HIV and AIDS, transmission, testing, prevention, treatment, viral load, CD4 and U=U. You do not need to know someone living with HIV to learn how to handle information more thoughtfully.
